catalog_quote: 8.2.9 Contrastive Accent. It is noteworthy that accent (often called “stress”, cf. Zorc 1979, 1993) is contrastive in Manide and Inagta Alabat, e.g., Manide, Alabat sáyug ‘river’ vs. Manide, Alabat sayúg ‘floor’, and Alabat káun /káʔun/ ‘eat’ vs. Alabat kaún /kaʔún/ ‘go to pick somebody up’.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage is verbatim at sec. 8.2.9, printed p. 259 of the held Lobel 2013 dissertation text (lines 9647-9650). Deciding source: a 2013 dissertation chapter by the language's primary fieldworker; it gives penult-vs-ultima minimal pairs (sáyug 'river' vs sayúg 'floor') and calls accent contrastive, with no positional/weight rule -> lexical is the faithful coding. it has no prosody section and its only stress remark (fn. 16) states that Manide retains contrastive stress, confirming the record and closing the second reader's open flag about Lobel 2010. sources.quote: 'positing Proto-Philippine forms allows for reconstructions with contrastive stress, which is retained in many Philippine languages (including Tagalog, Standard Bikol, and Manide) but has not been reliably reconstructed to PMP.' No default position, weight or length rule is given anywhere in the article.
